business_profile: LOZDEV is a website design, development, and hosting business. It builds fast, modern websites for small businesses and solo entrepreneurs, then hosts and maintains them so clients never have to think about the technical side. Voice: approachable, plain-spoken, confident - explain technical value in terms of business outcomes (more customers, less downtime, one less thing to worry about), not jargon.
target_audience: Small business owners and solo entrepreneurs who don't have a website yet, or have an old one that no longer represents them. Not deeply technical - they care about results (more customers, less hassle), not how the tech works.

style_examples:
The “Wait… We Actually Built This?” Post
There’s something uniquely satisfying about looking at a problem that used to take hours and realizing you’ve turned it into a button. 😅
I’ve been spending a lot of time lately thinking about how we build software—not just whether something works, but whether it makes the next problem easier to solve. The best systems I’ve worked on aren’t the ones with the most code. They’re the ones where six months later, you can still understand what past-you was thinking.
That’s probably my favorite part of engineering: taking something messy, pulling on the right thread, and watching the whole thing start to make sense. Sometimes the biggest wins aren’t flashy features. Sometimes they’re just making tomorrow’s problem slightly less annoying than today’s.

The “Engineering Is Weird” Post
Software engineering is one of the only jobs where you can spend three hours trying to fix something, discover that the problem was a typo, and somehow walk away feeling like you’ve just unlocked an ancient secret.
The older I get as a developer, the more I appreciate that engineering isn’t really about knowing every answer. It’s about being comfortable not knowing the answer yet. Read the documentation. Follow the logs. Question your assumptions. Break the problem into smaller problems. And, occasionally, stare at the screen long enough that the bug becomes embarrassed and fixes itself.
The fun part is that there’s always another rabbit hole. New language, new architecture, new database, new AI model, new ridiculous production issue waiting at 2:13 PM on a Friday. And honestly? That constant curiosity is probably the best part of the job.

The “AI Changed My Question” Post
I used to think the most interesting question in AI was, “What can the model do?” Lately, I’ve been much more interested in a different question: “How do we know when it’s right?”
That shift changes everything. Suddenly you’re thinking about confidence, context, sources, evaluation, hallucinations, observability, and all the little signals hiding underneath a seemingly simple answer. Building something that generates an answer is one problem. Building something that can explain, evaluate, and learn from the quality of that answer is a much more interesting one.
That’s the rabbit hole I’ve been enjoying lately. The more I work with AI systems, the less I think the future is about simply making models smarter—and the more I think it’s about building better systems around them. The model is only one piece of the puzzle.
